title: 4 Events in Seoul & Incheon You Shouldn't Miss This Month (Late October 2026)
html:
If you happen to be in the Seoul area in the next few weeks, you're in luck. From a cozy theater festival to a dog sports day, a huge ceramics show, and a vintage flea market by the sea, there's a lot going on that doesn't need any special planning — just show up. Here are four events worth building a free afternoon around, all easy to reach from Seoul.

1. D.FESTA Small Theater Festival (until October 25)

Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (TourAPI)

Korea has a whole neighborhood built around small theaters, and this festival is the best time to see why. Daehangno (literally "University Street") in Jongno-gu, Seoul, is packed with tiny stages that have been putting on plays for decades, and every year this festival brings in shows from all over the country — and sometimes from other countries too. You don't need to understand Korean to enjoy a lot of these: look for shows tagged as physical theater, dance, or ones with English subtitles.

Tickets are 30,000 won for adults and 15,000 won for students, and showtimes vary a lot by performance (evenings on weekdays, usually two or three showtimes on weekends). How to get there: take the subway to Hyehwa Station (Line 4), Exit 2 — Daehangno starts right outside the exit, so you can't really miss it.

💡 Local tip: like most theater and concert tickets in Korea, seats for popular shows get booked up through online ticketing sites days in advance, so it's smarter to check the festival's official site or Instagram (@koreasmalltheater) before you go, rather than just showing up and hoping for a walk-in seat.

2. Seoul Petlympics (October 24–25)

Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (TourAPI)

Exactly what it sounds like: a mini "Olympics" for dogs. At Peace Plaza inside Seoul World Cup Park (the park built around the 2002 World Cup stadium), dogs and their owners compete in beginner-friendly games — a "stay" challenge, a recall race, weaving through cones, and a short dash — plus there's a roughly 4 km group walk called the Dog Trail. If your dog is more of a spectator, you can still watch agility, frisbee, and even "dog dancing" demonstrations for free.

Watching is free; entering your own dog in an event costs around 40,000 won per event. The whole thing runs 10:00–17:00 both days. How to get there: World Cup Stadium Station (Line 6), Exit 1, then about a 10-minute walk through the park.

Even without a dog, this is a nice, low-key way to spend an afternoon outdoors and see a very different side of Seoul — Koreans take their pets seriously, and events like this show just how big pet culture has gotten here.

3. Gyeonggi Ceramics Biennale (until November 1)

Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (TourAPI)

Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (TourAPI)

Korea has been making ceramics — especially the pale green celadon pottery and white baekja porcelain you'll see in museums — for over a thousand years, and the towns around Icheon, Yeoju, and Gwangju in Gyeonggi-do are where a lot of today's potters still work. This biennale (a festival held every two years) spreads exhibitions and hands-on activities across all three towns, mixing traditional pieces with modern ceramic art.

It's a bit further out than the other events on this list — think day trip, not a quick subway ride. A combination ticket covering the main sites costs 11,000 won for adults, 7,000 won for children (free under 6 and for seniors 65+), and the main venue area is open 10:00–18:00. How to get there: the easiest way without a car is an intercity bus from Dong Seoul Bus Terminal (Gangbyeon Station, Line 2) to Icheon, which takes a little over an hour.

This one is best for travelers who already like pottery, museums, or just want to see a slower, countryside side of Korea outside Seoul.

4. Oh Slow Vintage Market (October 24–25)

Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (TourAPI)

If you like thrifting or flea markets, this one's worth the trip to Incheon. Around 70 vintage sellers from across Korea set up at Incheon Art Platform, a cluster of early-1900s brick warehouses turned into galleries and studios in the old Incheon Open Port area. Expect racks of vintage clothing, old accessories, retro odds and ends, and handmade goods, plus street busking and DJ sets to keep the mood lively. Admission is free, running 11:00–18:00 both days.

How to get there: Incheon Station (Line 1, the very last stop on the line) — Incheon Art Platform is a short walk from the station, and it sits right next to Incheon's Chinatown, so you can easily combine both in one day.

💬 Got your eye on one of these? Tell us which one in the comments — happy to help with directions, tickets, or anything else you're wondering about!
meta_description: 4 fun things to do in Seoul & Incheon this October: a theater festival, dog sports day, ceramics biennale, and vintage market.
